Observation_Details: One of two kites was carrying nesting material three times to a treetop. On 31 August 2023. O’Loghlen and Pam observed a Kite perched in Euc near the nest . It foraged in the field east of the Euc grove and very quickly caught what looked like a vole. It flew back to the nest area and gave the vole to a what presumably was a female. She quickly consumed it and flew off immediately - again I presume to the nest. On 18 Sept 2023, Jeff Hanson arrived at 9:15, spent 45 minutes checking on kites. Adult was perched on the large dead eucalyptus, his favorite perching tree. Shortly after I arrived, he went on a hunting foray in the far northern part of the eastern grasslands, very close to the Oaks that line Covington. A successful first strike. Through a scope, in 10 min I saw him eat the vole from the top down. He consumed the bottom half in one big gulp. I then trained the scope on the nest. Luckily there was very little wind. I finally figured out that I was looking at her tail sticking up in the air, behind sticks and leaves. She was pointing northwest, and literally did not move. On 23 Sept 2023, Mooney saw male chase a Red-tailed Hawk, pecking at the hawk’s wing until it left the area. At times the RTHA had its talons down. The kite then perched high in a dead tree, vocalized harshly, and made a big display of wingspread for several minutes. Assume female was on the nest, but couldn’t see her.
Comments: Northeast corner of lake. The two kites were in constant communication.

In the second display I saw two males and one female. In the third display I saw two females and one male. Best summary of phenology results are found in CCBER file Tricolored Blackbird data Sedgwick 2022.docx and it comes from Wendy Schackwitz, Point Blue Conservation Science, Research Associate, and her acoustics study (I.e., stage of breeding is determined by changes in vocalizations from the colony). To summarize: There were 2 broods. The first pulse had babies hatching around 17 April, and this would put fledging at around 14 days later. Observation_Details: At least two nests in the colony. On 8 July, London notes activity in 2, possibly 4 nest holes.

Observation_Details: Several Cedar Waxwings foraging (some sallying) from the top of a large pine. Then group of at least 4 flew down to lower tree where I got a better look and was able to get several photos. I did not see a begging/feeding event. Group behaved like a typical pair with fledged young following adults.
Comments: Between Holes 14-15. Adults: yellowish brown, medium crest, black eyeline and bill (mask), yellow tail tip. Pretty distinctive. Fledglings: (Refer to 6 photos in https://ebird.org/checklist/S114907874). I assert that there are at least two fledglings evidenced by different tail shape between first 3 photos (1 fledgling) and last photo (2nd fledgling). Streaked breast, grayish overall, crest, small bill, and whitish face with incomplete mask. At least one of the chicks was still feathering out, so it seems unlikely they would have flown in from any distance. In my opinion, it all indicates a LOCAL breeding event. I've seen Cedar Waxwings in this same pine in June in previous seasons. [EDITOR: First County breeding record.]

Observation_Details: Low numbers of birds first recorded Feb 8. Numbers building steadily. On 12 April, a high count of 500. On March 8 and 17, collection of apparent nest building materials was recorded. On 14 April, heavy foraging activity, as though there may be nestlings to feed. On May 3, the first fledgling was detected. The steady movement of adults out to forage and carrying food back to the colony was very apparent this same week. Fledglings dispersing on 17 and 24 May. A few fledglings and attendant adults lingered through mid June. On 21 June, Schneekloth saw none.
Comments: There is no real evidence of pond use during non breeding periods; in the winter European Starling/ Red-winged Blackbirds take over. Best summary of phenology results are found in CCBER file Tricolored Blackbird data Sedgwick 2023.docx and it comes from Wendy Schackwitz,Point Blue Conservation Science, Research Associate, and her acoustics study (I.e., stage of breeding is determined by changes in vocalizations from the colony). Pop size data come from the in-person observations. Those range from 150 to 500 reflecting the difficulty of obtaining counts of TrBl when RwBl are present.
